{{Short description|Shape in mathematics}}
[[Image:DataClustering ElbowCriterion.JPG|thumb|right|300px|Explained variance. The "elbow" is indicated by the red circle. The number of clusters chosen should therefore be 4.]]

[[Image:Solar-Cell-IV-curve-with-MPP.png|thumb|Photovoltaic solar cell I-V curves where a line intersects the knee of the curves where the maximum power transfer point is located.]]

In [[mathematics]], a '''knee of a curve''' (or '''elbow of a curve''') is a point where the curve visibly bends, specifically from high slope to low slope (flat or close to flat), or in the other direction. This is particularly used in [[Mathematical optimization|optimization]], where a knee point is the optimum point for some decision, for example when there is an [[increasing function]] and a trade-off between the benefit (vertical [[y axis|''y'' axis]]) and the cost (horizontal [[x axis|''x'' axis]]): the knee is where the benefit is no longer increasing rapidly, and is no longer worth the cost of further increases – a cutoff point of [[diminishing returns]].

In [[heuristic]] use, the term may be used informally, and a knee point identified visually, but in more formal use an explicit [[objective function]] is used, and depends on the particular optimization problem. A knee may also be defined purely geometrically, in terms of the [[curvature]] or the [[second derivative]].

== Definitions ==
The knee of a curve can be defined as a [[Vertex (curve)|vertex]] of the graph. This corresponds with the graphical intuition (it is where the curvature has a maximum), but depends on the choice of scale.

The term "knee" as applied to curves dates at least to the 1910s,<ref>{{cite book
|title=An Experimental Investigation of a New System for Automatically Regulating the Voltage of an Alternating Current Circuit
|first=John Alan
|last=Terrell
|publisher=Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute
|year=1913
|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=x4MoUp4tm1kC&q=knee+of+a+curve 10]
|quote=... enables one to tell how near the “knee” of the curve the iron is ...
}}</ref>
and is found more commonly by the 1940s,<ref>{{cite book
|title=NACA Wartime Report
|series=L
|year=1943
|publisher=[[National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics]]
|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=-GlDAQAAIAAJ&dq=knee%20of%20a%20curve&pg=PA21 21]
|quote=... the knee of the curve lies in the region of the critical load ...
}}</ref> being common enough to draw criticism.{{sfn|Worthing|Geffner|1943|loc=Preface}}<ref name="Kiokemeister">{{cite journal
|first=Fred L.
|last=Kiokemeister
|year=1949
|title=An Analysis of Functions Describing Experimental Data
|journal=Psychophysical Research
|page=[https://books.google.com/books?id=J5aednsGRY4C&dq=%22knee%20of%20a%20curve%22&pg=PA5 5]
}}</ref> The unabridged ''[[Webster's Dictionary]]'' (1971 edition) gives definition 3h of ''knee'' as:{{sfn|Thomas|Sheldon|1999|p=18}}
{{quotation|an abrupt change in direction in a curve (as on a graph); ''esp'' one approaching a right angle in shape.}}

== Criticism ==
Graphical notions of a "knee" of a curve, based on curvature, are criticized due to their dependence on the coordinate scale: different choices of scale result in different points being the "knee". This criticism dates at least to the 1940s, being found in {{harvtxt|Worthing|Geffner|1943|loc=Preface}}, who criticize:<ref name="Kiokemeister" />
{{quotation|references to the significance of a so-called knee of a curve when the location of the knee was a function of the chosen coordinate scales}}

== Detection methods ==

=== Kneedle algorithm ===
The Kneedle algorithm detects the best balanced tradeoff based on the mathematical [[curvature]] concept, which is defined and well studied for continuous functions.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Satopaa |first1=Ville |last2=Albrecht |first2=Jeannie |last3=Irwin |first3=David |last4=Raghavan |first4=Barath |chapter=Finding a "Kneedle" in a Haystack: Detecting Knee Points in System Behavior |title=2011 31st International Conference on Distributed Computing Systems Workshops |date=June 2011 |pages=166–171 |doi=10.1109/ICDCSW.2011.20|isbn=978-1-4577-0384-3 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Kleine |first1=Daniel |title=Detecting knee- / elbow points in a graph |url=https://towardsdatascience.com/detecting-knee-elbow-points-in-a-graph-d13fc517a63c |website=Medium |language=en |date=20 January 2023}}</ref> Alternatively, the kneepointDetection() function<ref>{{cite web |title=kneepointDetection: Fits 2 regression lines to data to estimate the knee (or... in SamSPECTRAL: Identifies cell population in flow cytometry data. |url=https://rdrr.io/bioc/SamSPECTRAL/man/kneepointDetection.html |website=rdrr.io |language=en}}</ref> from the SamSPECTRAL<ref>{{cite web |title=SamSPECTRAL |url=https://bioconductor.org/packages/SamSPECTRAL/ |website=Bioconductor}}</ref> [[R (programming language)|R]] package can be used to find the knee point, where is a "phase change" in the data, by fitting two lines using linear regression.
